proposals.relationship: Burton identifies Spivak’s feminist critique of archival recovery in “The Rani of Sirmur” as a formative resource for her account of feminism and imperial history.
proposals.evidence_note: Burton’s own 2011 retrospective recalls reading the 1985 Rani essay as a graduate student and explains its challenge to universal historical recovery and liberal imperial feminism. Do not silently substitute the later “Can the Subaltern Speak?” essay for this encounter, infer personal mentorship, or treat Burton’s retrospective as a complete restatement of Spivak’s position. Selected retrospective pages read; the complete original Spivak essay was not freshly read.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, pp. 4–6, especially identification of the 1985 essay on p. 4 and the recovery/disciplinary argument on pp. 5–6 (PDF 27–29).

proposals.relationship: Burton credits Said’s Orientalism with major importance for her intellectual and political formation while retaining her feminist criticism of its treatment of gender.
proposals.evidence_note: This is Burton’s explicit assessment, not shared postcolonial vocabulary. She recalls reading Orientalism the year before the 1985 Rani encounter. The positive debt coexists with the separate gender criticism; it does not endorse Said’s entire argument. Selected retrospective read; Said’s original book was not freshly read.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, pp. 4–5 (PDF 27–28), paragraph crossing the page break and the following gender comparison.

proposals.relationship: Burton criticizes Said’s inadequate engagement with women, gender and feminist analysis while explicitly acknowledging Orientalism’s importance to her own formation.
proposals.evidence_note: This is Burton’s particular feminist criticism in her own retrospective, not rejection of Orientalism wholesale. She contrasts Spivak’s feminist starting point with this limit. Selected primary retrospective read; no original Said-body reading or reply by Said is claimed.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, p. 5 (PDF 28), first full paragraph comparing Orientalism and Spivak’s feminist critique.

proposals.relationship: Burton uses Stuart Hall’s conjunctural framework to interpret domestic imperial culture as a historically contingent problem space requiring strategic intervention.
proposals.evidence_note: Her p. 6 explicitly names Hall and defines the framework before applying it to her own trajectory. This supports a particular conceptual use, not personal mentorship inferred from Hazel Carby’s Birmingham connection. Footnote 9’s original source is outside the preview and has not been independently read; no independent quotation-authentication of Hall is claimed.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, p. 6, second paragraph, note 9 and its immediate application (PDF 29).

proposals.relationship: Burton uses Scott’s critique of the evidence of experience and her account of gender as an effect of power to explain her own situated interpretation of empire.
proposals.evidence_note: The retrospective explicitly attributes the experience critique to Scott on p. 10, then borrows Scott’s produced-gender analysis on p. 14. Burton refuses a view of her own position as transparent or fully knowable. Her subsequent account of performativity also credits Judith Butler and Bernard Cohn; it is not Scott’s sole creation. No personal mentoring or full original Scott-body reading is inferred.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, p. 10 opening paragraph and p. 14 first paragraph (PDF 33 and 37).

proposals.relationship: Burton identifies Catherine Hall’s feminist remapping of home and empire as consequential to her imperial-history project, including the gendered imperial setting of political reform and Civilizing Subjects.
proposals.evidence_note: Burton explicitly connects Hall’s critique of public/private separation with home/empire and discusses work done partly with Keith McClelland and Jane Rendall, whose credit is retained. Civilizing Subjects is Hall’s separate monograph. This is Burton’s own methodological evaluation and resource statement, not cofield influence or sole authorship of collaborative work. Original Hall books were not freshly read.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, p. 12 second paragraph through p. 13 opening (PDF 35–36), notes 28–29 outside the preview.

proposals.relationship: Burton says that refracting gender-and-power insights through Butler’s work helped her understand nation and empire as performatively produced.
proposals.evidence_note: The same sentence gives Bernard Cohn’s anthropological history equal, distinct credit, with his durbar example; Cohn has no current endpoint and is recorded as a hold. The claim is a joint intellectual resource acknowledged by Burton, not sole Butler authorship of her entire method or a personal collaboration. Original Butler and Cohn works were not freshly read.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, p. 14 first paragraph, especially the sentence beginning Refracting these insights (PDF 37).

proposals.relationship: Burton draws on Stoler’s emphasis on colonial regimes’ precarious vulnerability when explaining why imperial culture should not be treated as an irresistible juggernaut.
proposals.evidence_note: Burton explicitly pairs Stoler’s formulation with John Darwin’s chaotic pluralism as interpretive postures making room for agency and resistance while retaining empire’s coercive power. Darwin’s co-credit is preserved; he has no current endpoint. This is a bounded conceptual use, not general agreement with every Stoler argument, personal mentoring, or a body-reading claim for Along the Archival Grain.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, p. 12 opening paragraph, note 27 outside the preview (PDF 35).

proposals.relationship: Burton explicitly borrows Gilroy’s formulation of interdependent modalities to describe how race, gender and class structured lived imperial Englishness.
proposals.evidence_note: This is a particular, expressly acknowledged conceptual borrowing in Burton’s discussion of Catherine Hall and feminist history, not a general assertion that all her work derives from Gilroy or a personal relationship. The original Gilroy text behind note 30 is outside the preview and was not freshly read.
primary_locators: Imperial Optics, pp. 12–13, sentence crossing the page break that expressly borrows from Paul Gilroy (PDF 35–36).

proposals.relationship: Burton criticizes Ornamentalism’s novelty claim and its failure to sustain an analysis of metropole–colony interdependence, arguing that it misreads Sinha’s and Catherine Hall’s accounts of empire’s constitutive role in domestic Britain.
proposals.evidence_note: Specific criticism in Burton’s own 2002 opening, reproduced as substantive authorial prose under Abstract on a third-party bibliographic page. She acknowledges Cannadine’s citations and declared interconnected model before criticizing its analytical limits. Sinha and Catherine Hall retain their distinct intellectual credit; neither is presented as a coauthor of Burton’s critique. The reproduced opening was freshly read, but the full article, original journal facsimile, Cannadine’s book and the original works of Sinha/Hall were not freshly read. No claim about the article’s unseen conclusion, a personal reply by Cannadine, or a complete rejection of every part of his work.
primary_locators: Déjà Vu All Over Again (2002), third-party reproduced opening under Abstract: paragraphs beginning The preface to the book, This new history, Hardly original, and For Marshall and Cannadine; selected following sentences on Sinha/Hall. Exact journal pagination or paragraph numbering not asserted.
